The ending feels completely natural and earned because it directly resolves the central tension established at the beginning of the story. The first half of the narrative builds up Q as a mythical figure possessing a "preternatural inability to experience social friction," while the narrator wonders how Q would handle unpleasant tasks like firing someone with "velvet-gloved ruthlessness." The climax at the beach club directly answers this question by exposing Q's charm as a hollow facade that fails completely when confronted with adult reality and a competent, direct subordinate. The final lines provide a strong sense of thematic closure and complete the narrator's arc, freeing him from his long-held inferiority complex as he realizes that "gravity on Earth was uniform after all."
